attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the universal 'every single' and the present-tense sales claim. The wording is heavily evaluative and borders on rhetoric, but it does assert a present state of affairs.

contract.note: The plain reading (misleading representations or omissions across all LLM products) is ordinary. The support condition requires coverage of the whole class and a single product can contradict, which fits the universal wording. But the speaker names no false representation and no time span for 'long term', so the result turns on the evaluator's reading.

evidence.note: Anthropic's terms say the service will change. This is a company disclosure. A contractual disclaimer alone does not settle whether the marketing was misleading.
OpenAI's terms say prices may change. This qualifies any idea of permanent pricing but says nothing about marketing claims across all products.

reviews.rationale: The packet holds only two companies' terms of service, both context. Nothing documents misleading sales claims across every LLM product, and nothing shows one product as a clear counterexample. The evidence available by the cutoff does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The firm 'will' clauses are kept as a forecast. The present-tense economics clause is handled separately, which is acceptable. No deadline was stated.

contract.note: Requiring both higher prices and workflow-breaking limits at both providers is a fair reading of the conjunction. Matching plans and currencies and leaving out new optional tiers is ordinary. 'Current workflows' and 'prices' are evaluator readings.

evidence.note: OpenAI's help page: Pro 200 keeps its $200 price but gets a lower usage allowance, which takes effect for existing subscribers only after the evaluation date. It shows no workflow made impossible.
Anthropic raised subscription usage limits in September 2026. This runs against the forecast but cannot disprove a forecast with no deadline.
Regional App Store price realignment: up in Korea, down elsewhere. An isolated regional change is not enough under the contract, and it carries no workflow evidence.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, and the contract's early-resolution rule is not met. No implemented change shows both a price rise and workflow-breaking limits at both providers. OpenAI's allowance cut takes effect after the cutoff, Anthropic raised limits, and the Korean price rise is regional only.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Will always hallucinate' and the 'not trustworthy as a result' inference are kept. The determinism clause is a separate claim, and 'unforgivable' is normative, so leaving both out is correct.

contract.note: Reading 'always hallucinate' as a lasting propensity rather than every answer being false is fair and ordinary. Refusing to let limited benchmarks decide the claim either way is appropriate. 'Trustworthy' is undefined by the speaker.

evidence.note: Kalai et al.: hallucinations persist in current systems, but the paper ties this to training and evaluation incentives. It does not show inevitability.
Suzuki et al. accept the formal inevitability result on infinite input sets but argue hallucinations can be made statistically negligible. This is mixed theory, not decisive.
Falcon produced zero hallucinations on 70 prompts. Under the contract, a finite benchmark cannot eliminate the propensity.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. No validated counterexample exists, and no impossibility result's assumptions clearly cover ordinary uses, so the early-resolution rule is not met. The theory points both ways and the benchmark is finite, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Cannot be deterministic' is a flat claim that determinism is impossible, and it is kept as such.

contract.note: 'Deterministic' in its ordinary technical sense (same input gives same output under fixed conditions) is a fair plain reading of 'cannot'. The speaker did not limit the claim to the default behaviour of hosted chatbots.

evidence.note: Thinking Machines (Sept 2025, before the post) got 1000 identical completions using batch-invariant kernels, with the implementation and code released. It was not independently rerun, but it is a primary engineering demonstration.

reviews.rationale: Before the post, a documented implementation produced identical repeated outputs under fixed conditions. That directly contradicts the claim that LLMs cannot be deterministic. The one caveat is that no independent party has reproduced the result.
